text: Drift is what happens when the real infrastructure in the cloud no longer matches what Terraform's state file believes is there. The usual cause isn't exotic: an on-call engineer gets paged at 2 a.m., something needs to change right now, and the fastest path is clicking directly in the console instead of opening a pull request and waiting for review. The fix works — but Terraform's state still records the old configuration, and nothing about the next plan says so on its own.

Left undetected, that compounds in two directions: the next pipeline apply might silently revert the urgent manual fix, since as far as Terraform knows the old configuration is still correct, and the team's mental model of what's actually running slowly drifts away from what the dot-tf files describe. The fix is running terraform plan even when nothing in the repository has changed, on a recurring schedule — cron: zero six star star star runs it every day at 06:00 UTC, with workflow_dispatch adding a manual run on demand.

detailed-exitcode is the flag that makes this whole pattern work. A plain terraform plan always exits zero whether or not anything changed, but detailed-exitcode returns zero for no changes, one for an error, and two specifically when the plan found real differences — exactly the did-reality-drift-from-state signal this job needs, captured into GITHUB_OUTPUT so a later step can read it.

Checking for that exit code equal to two and failing the job is what turns a plan nobody would otherwise read into a pipeline failure the team actually notices — a red, failed Nightly Drift Check run is a far more reliable alert than hoping someone remembers to run plan by hand next week. From there, the fix is deliberate: either codify the manual change into the configuration on purpose, or apply to put the resource back the way the files say it should be.

That closes out this chapter's whole arc: plan posted automatically on every pull request, apply gated behind a real approval, credentials and sensitive values handled correctly in between, and drift caught on a schedule instead of discovered by accident. Chapter 8 puts all four lessons to work in one real project, starting with building a reusable network module other environments can share.
